description: Question: why do two stars of the same colour differ a hundredfold in brightness? Idea: the Stefan–Boltzmann law, L = 4πR²σT⁴: a star's light is its surface temperature to the fourth power times its area. A random sample of 3,000 Gaia DR3 stars with parallaxes better than 5% (Gaia's TAP service, gaia_source joined with astrophysical_parameters) gives brightness, distance and temperature; Polars turns them into luminosity (inverse-square law, extinction, Gaia's bolometric correction BC_G(Teff) of Andrae et al. 2018) and into a radius R = √L (5772 K/T)². Our luminosities agree with Gaia's FLAME values to 0.03 dex (they use the same recipe) and our radii with GSP-Phot's spectral fit to 0.055 dex (log–log slope 0.97, a 7% median offset). On the HR diagram the dashed lines of constant radius sort the stars: at 4,800 K a dwarf and a giant differ by 10× in radius and 100× in light. The main sequence is a mass sequence: L ∝ M^4.7 here. Caveats: Teff from GSP-Phot is biased for some stars (hot, reddened); the bolometric correction is fitted only for 3,300–8,000 K, so other stars are left out; a parallax-limited sample over-represents luminous giants (Malmquist bias); FLAME masses are model-based. Next: binaries with dynamical masses (Gaia's nss_two_body_orbit), or ages across the main-sequence turn-off.
name: Stefan–Boltzmann on the HR diagram
